title: Coughing After Drinking Alcohol: 7 Causes and How to Stop It
excerpt: Why you cough after drinking alcohol, including reflux, sulfites in wine, histamine, and asthma triggers, plus why it gets worse at night and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why you cough after drinking alcohol: reflux, sulfites in wine, histamine, and asthma triggers. Why it's worse at night and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** most coughing after drinking comes from one of three things. The first is **acid reflux**, because alcohol loosens the valve that keeps stomach acid out of your throat. The second is a **reaction to something in the drink**, most often sulfites in wine or histamine in wine and beer. The third is plain **irritation**: strong spirits, carbonation, a dry throat, or a smoky room. For most social drinkers it's harmless and fixable by changing what, how fast, and how late you drink. The exception is coughing that comes with wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing, which can mean alcohol is triggering asthma or an allergic-type reaction and deserves a doctor's attention.

This guide walks through each cause, how to tell them apart, what to do about coughing after wine or beer, why it often gets worse at night, and the signs that mean you should get help rather than wait it out.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 right away if** coughing after a drink comes with trouble breathing, wheezing that doesn't settle, throat tightness, swelling of the lips, tongue or face, hives spreading across the body, or feeling faint. Those can be signs of a serious allergic reaction. **Also call 911 if** someone who has been drinking heavily is choking, vomiting while very drowsy, or can't be woken properly; roll them onto their side while you wait. **See a doctor soon if** you cough up blood, have chest pain, develop a fever and a wet cough after vomiting while drunk (this can mean vomit went into the lungs), have a cough that lasts more than three weeks, or reliably wheeze or get short of breath after drinking. If you have asthma, tell your doctor that alcohol is a trigger for you.

## Why Do I Cough When I Drink Alcohol? The Main Causes

Coughing is a reflex. Your airway is lined with nerves that react to anything that shouldn't be there, whether that's acid, a chemical irritant, mucus dripping down from your nose, or an airway that has tightened up. Alcohol can set off that reflex through several routes, and more than one can be in play on the same night.

Here are the common ones, roughly in order of how often they're the culprit:

1. **Acid reflux** (including the "silent" kind that reaches the throat without much heartburn)
2. **Sulfites**, mainly in wine, some ciders, and certain mixers
3. **Histamine and the body's reaction to alcohol's breakdown products**
4. **Alcohol-triggered asthma** in people with sensitive airways
5. **Direct irritation** from high-proof spirits, carbonation, or very cold drinks
6. **Postnasal drip** from a stuffy nose
7. **Your surroundings**: smoke, vaping, shouting over music, and a dry throat from dehydration

The sections below cover each one and the clues that point to it.

## Cause 1: Acid Reflux, the Most Common Culprit

At the top of your stomach sits a ring of muscle called the lower esophageal sphincter. Its job is to let food in and keep acid from coming back up. Alcohol relaxes that muscle, and it also increases stomach acid and can slow the stomach's emptying. Put those together and acid is more likely to travel upward.

Most people know reflux as heartburn: a burning feeling behind the breastbone. But acid and stomach contents can also reach the throat and voice box. Doctors call this laryngopharyngeal reflux, and it often causes little or no heartburn. Instead, people notice:

- A dry, tickly cough, often after a meal or when lying down
- Frequent throat clearing
- Hoarseness or a croaky voice the next morning
- A feeling of a lump in the throat
- A sour or bitter taste at the back of the mouth

Even small amounts of acid can irritate the sensitive tissue in the throat and trigger the cough reflex. Acid in the lower esophagus can also set off coughing through a nerve reflex, without ever reaching the throat.

**Clues it's reflux:** the cough starts after drinking with a meal, gets worse when you lie down, comes with heartburn, burping, or a sour taste, and is worse with wine, beer, fizzy mixers, or a big late dinner.

If this sounds like you, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains the reflux side in more detail, and our roundup of the [best antacids after drinking](/never-hungover/best-antacid-after-drinking) compares the over-the-counter options. Antacids can take the edge off an occasional bad night, but they don't fix the underlying trigger, and frequent reflux is worth discussing with a doctor.

## Cause 2: Sulfites in Wine (and Some Other Drinks)

Sulfites are preservatives. Winemakers use sulfur dioxide to stop spoilage and oxidation, and small amounts also form naturally during fermentation. In the US, wine containing 10 parts per million or more of sulfites must carry a "contains sulfites" label, which is why you see it on nearly every bottle.

For most people, sulfites cause no problems at all. But a minority of people are sensitive to them, and that sensitivity is much more common in people with asthma. When a sensitive person breathes in sulfur dioxide gas released from the drink, the airways can tighten. That can show up as:

- Coughing soon after the first few sips
- Chest tightness or a feeling of not getting a full breath
- Wheezing
- Less often, flushing or hives

White and sweet wines often contain more added sulfites than dry reds, which surprises a lot of people who blame red wine for everything. Dried fruit, some ciders, bottled lemon or lime juice, and certain cocktail mixers can also contain sulfites.

**Clues it's sulfites:** the cough starts quickly, within minutes of drinking, it's tied to wine or cider more than to clear spirits, you have asthma or a history of wheezing, and you may notice similar reactions to dried fruit or other preserved foods.

We cover sulfites in more depth, including how much different wines contain and what "low-sulfite" labels really mean, in our article on [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches).

## Cause 3: Histamine and Alcohol's Breakdown Products

Wine and beer contain histamine, a compound produced during fermentation. Red wines generally contain more than whites. Histamine is the same chemical your body releases in an allergic reaction, and it can cause a stuffy or runny nose, flushing, itching, and in some people a tight chest.

Two things make this worse with alcohol. First, alcohol appears to interfere with the enzyme that breaks down histamine in the gut (diamine oxidase, or DAO), so more of it gets into your system. Second, when your body breaks down alcohol, it produces a substance called acetaldehyde. Acetaldehyde can cause certain cells to release more of your own histamine. People who build up acetaldehyde quickly, including many people of East Asian descent with a common gene variant that slows its breakdown, are especially prone to flushing and, in some cases, alcohol-triggered asthma symptoms.

The result can be a cough that comes partly from your nose (postnasal drip) and partly from airways that have become twitchy.

**Clues it's histamine:** you get a stuffy nose, sneezing, flushed face, or itchy skin along with the cough, it's worse with red wine, aged beer, or fermented drinks, and you may react to aged cheese or cured meats too. Read more in our guides to [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) and [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance).

## Cause 4: When Alcohol Triggers Asthma

If you have asthma, alcohol can act as a trigger. Surveys of people with asthma have found that a meaningful share report their symptoms getting worse after drinking, with wine the drink most often blamed. The triggers are usually the sulfites and histamine described above, rather than the alcohol itself.

There's also a specific condition worth knowing about. **Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD)**, sometimes called Samter's triad, combines asthma, nasal polyps, and reactions to aspirin and similar painkillers. Research from specialists who treat it has found that most people with AERD report breathing symptoms such as nasal congestion and wheezing after even small amounts of alcohol. If you have asthma, nasal polyps, and you react to both aspirin and alcohol, that combination is worth mentioning to an allergist.

**Clues it's asthma-related:** the cough comes with wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath, you already have asthma or allergies, or the cough eases with your reliever inhaler.

If you have asthma, don't just push through these symptoms. Talk to your doctor about alcohol as a trigger. They may adjust your treatment plan or advise you on which drinks to avoid. If you carry a reliever inhaler, keep it with you on nights out.

## Cause 5: Irritation From Strong Spirits, Carbonation, and Cold

Sometimes the explanation is simple. High-proof alcohol is an irritant. A shot of neat whiskey, vodka, or a cask-strength spirit releases alcohol vapor as you swallow, and breathing that in can make you cough or sputter, especially if you drink it fast. That's the classic cough after a shot, and it usually passes in seconds.

Other irritants include:

- **Carbonation.** Bubbles expand your stomach and push gas and acid upward, so sparkling wine, beer, hard seltzers, and soda-based mixers can all feed reflux.
- **Very cold drinks.** Some people with sensitive airways cough after very cold or iced drinks, whether or not they contain alcohol.
- **Strong flavors.** Peppery, spicy, or citrus-heavy cocktails can tickle the throat, and acidic citrus adds to reflux.
- **Drinking "down the wrong pipe."** Alcohol dulls your swallowing reflexes, so a bit of liquid going into the airway is more likely when you've had a few. A brief coughing fit as your body clears it is normal.

**Clues it's irritation:** the cough is immediate, short, and linked to a specific drink or the way you drank it, and it doesn't come with other symptoms.

## Cause 6: Postnasal Drip From a Stuffy Nose

Alcohol widens blood vessels, including the ones lining your nose. That can leave you congested, and the extra mucus drains down the back of your throat. That drip is one of the most common causes of cough in general, and it's often worse lying down at night.

If your nose blocks up when you drink, see our guide to a [stuffy nose after drinking](/never-hungover/stuffy-nose-after-drinking), which covers why it happens and how to ease it.

## Cause 7: Smoke, Shouting, and a Dry Throat

It's easy to blame the drink when the surroundings are the real problem. A night out can mean:

- **Cigarette smoke or vaping**, either your own or other people's. Many people who rarely smoke do so only when drinking.
- **Talking loudly over music for hours**, which strains the throat and voice box.
- **Dehydration**, since alcohol makes you pass more urine, leaving your mouth and throat dry and scratchy.
- **Mouth breathing and snoring** after drinking, which dries the throat overnight.

If your cough mostly shows up the morning after, along with a raw or scratchy throat, these are likely contributors. Our article on [sore throat after drinking](/never-hungover/sore-throat-after-drinking) covers that side of things.

## Coughing After Drinking Wine

Wine gets its own section because it's the drink most often linked to coughing. It can hit several triggers at once:

- **Sulfites**, which can bother sensitive airways, particularly in people with asthma
- **Histamine**, which is usually higher in red wine and can cause congestion and postnasal drip
- **Acidity**, which can add to reflux
- **Sparkling wine's bubbles**, which combine carbonation with sulfites

What to try:

- **Switch styles for a few nights** and note what happens. If you cough with white wine but not with dry red, sulfites are a better suspect than histamine. If red bothers you more, histamine is more likely.
- **Try a clear spirit with a still, low-acid mixer** as a comparison. If the cough disappears, the issue is something in the wine rather than alcohol in general.
- **Don't count on "low-sulfite" or "natural" wines to fix it.** They can help some people, but all wine contains some sulfites, and they don't address histamine or reflux.
- **If wine reliably makes you wheeze, stop drinking it and talk to a doctor.** Sulfite reactions in people with asthma can be serious.

For more on red wine reactions in general, see our guide to [red wine headaches](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache).

## Coughing After Drinking Beer

Beer brings its own mix of triggers:

- **Carbonation and volume**, which can push acid up into your throat
- **Histamine and other fermentation compounds**, often higher in unfiltered and aged styles
- **Grains, hops, and yeast**, which a small number of people react to
- **Cold temperature and fast drinking**, which can irritate a sensitive throat

What to try:

- **Slow down and avoid chugging.** Gulping large amounts of cold, fizzy liquid is a near-perfect setup for reflux.
- **Notice the style.** If heavily hopped, aged, or unfiltered beers bother you more than a light lager, you may be reacting to an ingredient rather than the alcohol.
- **Avoid lying down soon after a few beers.**
- **If you get hives, an itchy mouth, or swelling with beer**, mention it to a doctor. A true allergy to a beer ingredient is uncommon but possible, and it's worth getting tested rather than guessing.

## Coughing at Night After Drinking

Many people only notice the cough when they get into bed, or they wake up coughing at 3 a.m. after a night out. A few things come together at night:

- **Reflux gets easier when you lie flat.** Gravity no longer helps keep acid down, and alcohol has already relaxed the valve at the top of your stomach.
- **A late meal adds pressure.** A full stomach plus alcohol plus lying down is the classic recipe for nighttime reflux.
- **Postnasal drip pools at the back of the throat** when you're lying down.
- **Alcohol disrupts sleep.** As it wears off in the second half of the night, sleep gets lighter and more broken, so you're more likely to wake up to a cough you might otherwise have slept through.

What helps:

- **Stop drinking two to three hours before bed** and avoid a heavy late meal.
- **Raise the head of your bed** a few inches, or sleep slightly propped up. Lying on your left side may also reduce reflux for some people.
- **Drink water** before bed to ease a dry throat.
- **If you wake up coughing with a burning throat or sour taste**, sit up for a while and sip water.

If nighttime coughing after drinking happens often, or you also snore heavily and wake up gasping, mention it to a doctor. Alcohol can make sleep-related breathing problems worse.

## Coughing Up Phlegm After Drinking

A wet cough with mucus after a night out usually comes from postnasal drip, irritation from smoke, or a cold you were already fighting. It typically clears within a day or two.

Take it more seriously if:

- **You cough up blood**, or mucus that's streaked with blood more than once
- **The phlegm is thick and green or brown and you have a fever**, especially if you were very drunk and may have vomited, since vomit breathed into the lungs can cause a chest infection called aspiration pneumonia
- **It lasts longer than three weeks**
- **You feel short of breath or have chest pain**

Those are reasons to see a doctor rather than wait it out.

## How to Tell Which Cause Is Yours

A simple way to narrow it down is to keep a short note on your phone for a few nights out: what you drank, how fast, whether you ate, when the cough started, and any other symptoms. Patterns usually show up quickly.

| What you notice | Most likely cause |
|---|---|
| Cough within minutes of wine or cider, maybe with chest tightness | Sulfites, especially if you have asthma |
| Stuffy nose, flushing, or itchy skin with the cough, worse with red wine | Histamine or alcohol intolerance |
| Cough after a meal or when lying down, with heartburn or sour taste | Acid reflux |
| Wheezing or shortness of breath with any alcohol | Alcohol-triggered asthma; see a doctor |
| Quick coughing fit after a shot or a gulp | Irritation or liquid going down the wrong way |
| Mostly the next morning, with a scratchy throat | Dehydration, smoke, shouting, mouth breathing |
| Hives, swelling, throat tightness | Possible allergic reaction; call 911 |

## Practical Ways to Stop Coughing After Drinking

Most of these cost nothing and work by removing the trigger rather than masking the symptom:

1. **Drink slower.** Sipping instead of gulping reduces reflux, irritation, and the chance of liquid going the wrong way.
2. **Eat beforehand, but not a huge late meal.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption, but a large, fatty, or spicy dinner right before bed feeds reflux.
3. **Pick still over sparkling.** Swap soda mixers for still options and see if it helps.
4. **Test your drink choice.** Compare a clear spirit with a still mixer against wine or beer to see which triggers you.
5. **Alternate with water.** It eases a dry throat and slows your overall pace.
6. **Avoid smoke.** Step away from smokers and skip the "only when I drink" cigarette.
7. **Finish drinking well before bed** and sleep with your head slightly raised.
8. **Keep your inhaler with you** if you have asthma, and talk to your doctor about alcohol as a trigger.

**A note on cough medicine.** If you already have a cold and you're coughing, be careful about combining alcohol with cough and cold remedies. Many contain dextromethorphan, antihistamines, or acetaminophen, and several of these can add to alcohol's sedating effects or put extra load on your liver. Some liquid cough syrups also contain alcohol themselves. Our guide to [cough medicine and alcohol](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) goes through which ingredients to watch for. When in doubt, ask a pharmacist.

## Is It an Alcohol Allergy?

People often wonder whether coughing after drinking means they're allergic to alcohol. True allergy to ethanol itself is rare. What's far more common is a sensitivity or intolerance to something in a particular drink (sulfites, histamine, grains, or fruit), or a reflux response. An allergist can help sort this out if your symptoms are bothersome or getting worse.

The one thing not to do is guess when symptoms include hives, swelling, or breathing trouble. Those can be signs of a genuine allergic reaction, and they need urgent medical care. Our guide to [alcohol allergy](/never-hungover/alcohol-allergy) explains the difference between allergy and intolerance and how each is diagnosed.

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

To be straightforward about it: there is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin) prevents or treats coughing after drinking. Coughing from reflux, sulfites, histamine, or asthma has its own causes, and a hangover supplement doesn't address them.

What DHM has been studied for is alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms more broadly. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Some people take it before a night out hoping for an easier morning. If you're curious, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you have asthma or take regular medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

For the cough itself, the steps above (slower drinking, still drinks, finishing early, and identifying your trigger) will do far more. And the most reliable way to have a better morning is still the basics in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Bottom Line

- Coughing after drinking is usually caused by **acid reflux**, **sulfites or histamine** in wine and beer, or **simple irritation** from spirits, bubbles, smoke, or a dry throat.
- **Wine** is the drink most often linked to coughing because it can combine sulfites, histamine, and acidity. **Beer** adds carbonation and volume.
- **Coughing at night** after drinking often points to reflux, made worse by lying down soon after drinking or eating.
- If coughing comes with **wheezing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath**, alcohol may be triggering asthma. Talk to your doctor.
- **Call 911** for trouble breathing, throat tightness, swelling, or spreading hives, or if a very drunk person is choking or can't be woken properly.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I cough after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reasons are acid reflux (alcohol relaxes the valve at the top of your stomach, so acid can reach your throat), a reaction to sulfites or histamine in wine and beer, and simple irritation from strong spirits, carbonation, or a dry throat. Smoky bars and late nights add to it. If you also wheeze or feel short of breath, the drink may be triggering asthma, which is worth raising with a doctor.

**Why do I cough after drinking wine but not other drinks?**

Wine is one of the highest-sulfite drinks people commonly have, and it also contains histamine, especially red wine. Some people, and particularly people with asthma, react to sulfites with coughing, chest tightness, or wheezing. Others react to histamine with a stuffy nose and postnasal drip that sets off a cough. Trying a different style of wine, or switching to a clear spirit for a night, can help you work out which it is.

**Why do I cough after drinking beer?**

Beer combines carbonation, which can push acid up into your throat, with histamine and other compounds from fermentation, plus barley and hops that a small number of people react to. Cold, fizzy beer drunk quickly is a classic reflux trigger. If beer reliably makes you cough or wheeze, note which styles do it and mention it to a doctor, since a true grain or hops allergy is possible but uncommon.

**Why do I cough at night after drinking?**

Lying down after drinking makes reflux more likely, because gravity is no longer helping keep stomach acid down and alcohol has already loosened the valve that holds it in. Acid reaching the throat while you sleep can cause a dry cough, hoarseness, or waking up coughing. Finishing drinks two to three hours before bed, avoiding a late heavy meal, and raising the head of your bed can help.

**Is coughing after drinking a sign of an alcohol allergy?**

Usually not. True allergy to alcohol itself is very rare. Most people who cough after drinking are reacting to reflux, sulfites, histamine, or an ingredient in a specific drink. But if coughing comes with hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, throat tightness, or trouble breathing, treat it as a possible allergic reaction and call 911.

**Can drinking alcohol make a cough worse?**

Yes. Alcohol can dry you out, worsen reflux, and disrupt sleep, all of which can keep a cough going. If you already have a cold or chest infection, drinking won't help it clear. Be especially careful about combining alcohol with cough or cold medicines, since many contain ingredients that add to alcohol's sedating effects.

**Will DHM stop me coughing after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats coughing after drinking. DHM is studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms, mostly in animal research with limited human data. It does not address reflux, sulfite sensitivity, or asthma triggered by alcohol, so it is not a substitute for managing those causes.
